What if a genuinely stable, growing field in healthcare didn't require a nursing degree, years of clinical training, or a single day of hospital experience to break into? You can't get hired without experience, and you can't get experience without being hired. title: Work Less, Not Faster: AI Automation for Beginners: Organize First, Then Scale. A 6-Step M
description: You've tried the AI tools. You watched the four-minute videos. And every Monday you're still building the same report by hand. It probably wasn't you. In 2025, researchers at MIT looked at how generative AI was performing inside real companies, with real budgets and real engineers. Ninety-five percent of them were getting no measurable return. The tools worked fine. What failed was everything around them: nobody had looked at the process before automating it. That is the trap. Automating a bad process just makes the waste run faster. It runs more often, it goes quiet, and nobody watches a machine. A book about AI automation that makes you wait for the AI Work Less, Not Faster is a step-by-step guide for beginners, and the tools don't show up until chapter seven. That is on purpose. Before you automate anything, you need a way of looking at your own work that you don't currently have. A group of factory engineers in postwar Japan built the best one anyone has come up with, and this book turns it on your desk, your inbox and your spreadsheets. The method has six steps, and they happen in a fixed order. The letters spell the word that gives the method its name: K. Know the work. Find where your task starts and ends, and go and watch it run. A. Axe the waste. Remove what doesn't need to exist before you build anything. I. Improve the design. Combine, reorder and simplify what's left. Z. Zero-touch. Now, and only now, let a machine do the steps that are rules. No coding required. E. Evaluate. Count the process and find out whether it worked. N. Now scale. Find the slowest step, leave room in it, and grow.
